reason: The story features a high-speed 'failed star' discovered by citizen scientists that is fast enough to escape our galaxy, backed by multiple reliable sources.
story: Everyday citizens just made a discovery that breaks the scales of galactic speed. Using NASA’s WISE mission data, volunteers with the Backyard Worlds project spotted a faint object named CWISE J1249+3621. It is an L subdwarf—a rare, low-mass object sitting right on the line between a star and a brown dwarf. But while most stars orbit the Milky Way at a steady pace, this one is screaming through space at over one million miles per hour. That is fast enough to completely break free from the Milky Way’s gravity and vanish into intergalactic space. Located just 400 light-years away, it is the closest hypervelocity star ever found. Astronomers believe it was either 'kicked' by a massive supernova or catapulted by a pair of black holes in a star cluster. This ancient relic, likely from the galaxy’s first generation of stars, is on a one-way trip out of our neighborhood forever.
angle: Citizen scientists discovered a 'failed star' screaming through the Milky Way at 1 million miles per hour, fast enough to escape our galaxy's gravity forever.

claims.claim: CWISE J1249+3621 is traveling at approximately 1 million miles per hour.
The object was discovered by citizen scientists participating in the Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 project.
It is moving fast enough to escape the Milky Way's gravity and enter intergalactic space.
The object is located approximately 400 light-years away from Earth.
Data for the discovery came from NASA's Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) mission.
CWISE J1249+3621 is classified as an L subdwarf.
The object's mass is estimated to be roughly 8% of the Sun's mass or about 80 times the mass of Jupiter.
It is the first hypervelocity object found with a mass similar to or less than a small star.
One theory for its speed is ejection from a binary system after a white dwarf companion exploded as a Type Ia supernova.
Another theory is that it was launched from a globular cluster after an encounter with a black hole binary.
The object contains significantly less iron and other metals than typical stars or brown dwarfs.
Its composition suggests it is very old, likely from the first generations of stars in the Milky Way.
Follow-up observations were conducted using the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii.
The discovery team included citizen scientists Martin Kabatnik and Thomas P. Bickle.
The star's speed is roughly 0.1% the speed of light.

disputed: The exact speed varies between sources, with S1 citing 280 miles per second and S3 citing 1.3 million miles per hour; the script should use 'about 1 million miles per hour' as a consensus.

The identity of the third citizen scientist varies, with S1 naming Austin Rothermich and S2/S7 naming Dan Caselden; the script should focus on the group as 'citizen scientists' or attribute names specifically.
